title: Group therapy formats
summary: An overview of three common group formats for adults: structured cognitive behavioral groups, dialectical behavior therapy skills groups (trained clinicians only), and interpersonal process groups. Covers screening, preparation, ground rules, co-leadership, confidentiality and telehealth groups.
whenToUse: When a group format fits the client's needs and preferences, or offers peer support individual work cannot.
When a guideline recommends group treatment first (for example group cognitive behavioral therapy for less severe depression).
When planning a new group or reviewing an existing one.

steps.heading: Choose the format
items: Structured cognitive behavioral groups: a set number of sessions, a shared curriculum, practice between sessions, and a leader who teaches and coaches.

Dialectical behavior therapy skills groups: weekly skills teaching in mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation and interpersonal effectiveness, usually alongside individual therapy and a consultation team. Trained clinicians only.
Interpersonal process groups: members learn from how they relate to each other in the group, with the leader drawing attention to here-and-now patterns.

steps.heading: Screen and prepare
items: Meet each person individually first to check fit, goals and readiness.
Ask about safety, current crises and anything that could make group unsafe for them or others.
Explain what will happen, group rules and what members can expect in the first sessions.

steps.heading: Set agreements
items: Confidentiality among members, and its limits (members are not bound the way clinicians are).
Attendance, lateness and contact between members outside the group.
Respect, speaking for yourself, and how to raise concerns.

steps.heading: Co-lead and run sessions
steps.body: Plan roles with your co-leader, debrief after each session, and keep a balance between structure and responsiveness. Build cohesion early: it is linked to better outcomes.

steps.heading: Monitor and follow up
steps.body: Use brief measures privately, check on members who withdraw or miss sessions, and offer individual follow-up when needed.

steps.heading: Telehealth groups
steps.body: Confirm each member's location and a backup number at every session, agree on privacy (no one else in the room, headphones), and have a plan if someone becomes unsafe while online.

prompts: In this group, what is said here stays here. I am bound by confidentiality, and I will ask each of you to agree to keep what others share private too.
I notice several people went quiet after that. What happened in the group just then?
Before we start, let's check in briefly: one word for how you are arriving today.
cautions: Group members cannot guarantee confidentiality; tell members this plainly and do not promise it.
Some people are not suited to group at a particular time (for example acute crisis or severe social anxiety without preparation); offer another format or preparation first.
Dialectical behavior therapy skills groups are part of a treatment program; delivering them without training and consultation is outside most clinicians' competence.
Never share one member's measures or disclosures with the group.

adaptations.adaptation: Keep groups smaller, use cameras on where possible, and assign one co-leader to watch the chat and members' wellbeing.
Consider groups in the members' own language or for people with shared identities, and adapt examples and materials.

evidenceSummary: NICE guideline NG222 (2022) recommends group cognitive behavioral therapy among first-line options for less severe depression. A 2016 meta-analysis (Burlingame and colleagues) found no significant outcome differences between individual and group formats when treatment, patients and dose were comparable. A 2018 meta-analysis (Burlingame, McClendon and Yang) found that group cohesion is associated with better outcomes. A 2015 trial (Linehan and colleagues) supports the skills training component of dialectical behavior therapy. The American Group Psychotherapy Association guidelines were updated in 2025 (Bernard and colleagues).
